title: Ubuntu/Botho — personhood through relationships
when: Ubuntu/Botho/Hunhu arises from long-standing southern African traditions; it has no single known founding date. Christian B. N. Gade traces the written term to at least 1846. Broader definitions as a philosophy or ethic developed later; the familiar proverb was used to explain ubuntu in writing around 1993–95.
people: No single founder is known. Modern interpreters include Mogobe B. Ramose, Thaddeus Metz, and Michael Onyebuchi Eze.
origin: Southern Africa, in related Bantu-language contexts: Nguni ubuntu, Sotho-Tswana botho, and Shona hunhu. Their histories differ; Ubuntu is not one doctrine shared uniformly across Africa.
idea: The Nguni saying umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu—“a person is a person through other persons”—captures a relational view: human capacities and moral personhood develop among others, not in isolation. In influential ethical reconstructions, actions are better when they express care and solidarity and sustain humane relationships; worse when they humiliate or fracture them. This is not simply obedience to a group or rejection of individuality.
relevance: Ubuntu informs healthcare, community decision-making, and restorative justice by asking whether institutions help people live well together. But critics debate how it protects autonomy and outsiders, and whether leaders can turn it into a political slogan. The test is whether relationships include, rather than marginalize, their members.

sources.name: Christian B. N. Gade, “The Historical Development of the Written Discourses on Ubuntu” (Aarhus University)
